There is a particular shade of blue that only exists for about twelve minutes, twice a day, if the weather is kind and you happen to be looking up. Not navy, not sky, not the theatrical violet of twilight—something quieter, like the color of a thought you almost remember. I think about that blue often. Not because it is beautiful, though it is, but because it refuses to stay. It is the definition of a temporary kingdom.

I find myself drawn lately to the architecture of in-between places: the landing on a stairwell, the parking garage at 3 a.m., the silence after someone says “I have to go now” but hasn’t moved yet. These are the rooms of our lives that don’t appear on any floor plan. They are where the real negotiations happen—the ones with yourself.

Last week I watched a spider rebuild a web in the corner of a window I never open. It worked with the patience of something that has never heard of a deadline. Every morning the web was broken—wind, rain, a careless elbow—and every evening it was back, more intricate, as if the spider was not repairing damage but refining an argument. I don’t know what the argument was. Maybe that persistence itself is a kind of language, one that doesn’t need an audience. Maybe the web was never meant for catching anything. Maybe it was just a way of saying: *I was here. I am still here. Here is the shape of my attention.*

We talk so much about presence these days, as if it were a light switch. Be present. Stay present. But presence, I think, is more like weather. You can’t force it; you can only notice the conditions. Sometimes it arrives as a sudden clarity—the smell of rain on hot asphalt, the exact weight of a book in your hands. Sometimes it hides inside boredom, inside the long wait for a train that is running late. Those are the moments that ask the most of you, because there is nothing to distract you from yourself.

I want to live in a way that makes room for these moments. Not the highlight reel, not the documented ones, but the unremarkable ones. The cup of tea that cools too slowly. The stranger who holds the door a second longer than necessary. The way a song sounds different at four in the morning, not because the song changed, but because you have.

We are always becoming someone, and that someone is made of these small, uncelebrated choices: whether to rush, whether to notice, whether to stay in the discomfort of not knowing. There is no final version of yourself waiting at the end of a to-do list. There is only this version, now, reading these words, carrying whatever weather you brought with you.

So if you are tired, let this be a place to rest for a moment. If you are restless, let this be permission to wander. The blue will come back in a little while, if you are near a window. And even if you miss it—especially if you miss it—there will be something else. There always is. The world is generous that way, though it never promises to be loud about it.

Go gently. The in-between is where we live, after all.
